title: When Do Graph Neural Rankers Need Partial Orders? A Diagnostic and Predictive Framework for Poset-Aware Ranking
content: Graph neural network (GNN) approaches to ranking and pairwise comparison recovery, most notably GNNRank [15], and standard learning-to-rank pipelines almost universally reduce a collection of items to a single global scalar score per item, i.e. a total order. Real comparison data, however, is frequently and genuinely partial: two items can be structurally incomparable given the available evidence, not merely tied or unranked. This paper introduces a three-metric diagnostic framework—the Cycle Inconsistency Rate (CIR), the Transitive Redundancy Rate (TRR), and the Structural Incomparability Rate (SIR)—for auditing how totally-orderable a comparison dataset actually is, computed directly from data before any ranking model is fit. In a systematic synthetic study spanning six controlled settings with five random seeds each, we show that SIR predicts, in a specific non-monotonic (inverted-U) relationship between means, whether a partial-order-aware GNN ranker outperforms a total-order (single-score) baseline: a robust, sign-stable advantage at moderate incomparability (SIR approx. 50%), and a smaller, seed-unstable advantage at high incomparability. We validate both regimes on real data with matching multi-seed resampling protocols. Four real graph-structured datasets spanning citation, hyperlink, and co-purchase networks (all at SIR > 90%) independently reproduce the high-SIR sign instability found synthetically. A real dataset of National Basketball Association (NBA) player statistics from the skyline-query database literature, selected to sit at SIR approx. 49%, reproduces the moderate-SIR advantage across four independently-chosen dimension pairs, the most consistently replicated finding in this work. A second real dataset from a different domain (real-estate records) at comparable SIR shows a weaker, noisier effect, which we trace to a complementary, secondary condition—how informative the available item features are about the underlying comparison criteria—rather than to any weakness in SIR itself; a controlled seven-point synthetic study that isolates feature informativeness from SIR confirms this directly, showing a close-to-monotonic relationship between feature informativeness and model advantage at fixed SIR. We further provide algorithmic descriptions of both the partial-order-aware architecture and its total-order counterpart, situate the latter within the GNNRank lineage, and report a complete, reproducible dataset inventory. The result is a diagnostic framework with real-world-validated predictive power across the full range of incomparability it characterizes, directly actionable as a pre-modeling triage step for practitioners choosing between ranking-model families.
